avis.abstract: available 54 55 Pregnant Sprague-Dawley rats received by oral gavage BHA dissolved in corn oil from GD 7- 56 17 at doses of 250, 500, 750 or 1000 mg/kg bw/d. In dams, a dose-dependent increase in 57 relative liver and stomach weights was observed (no further details). BHA did not lead to any 23 SCCS/1682/25 Preliminary version Scientific advice on the safety of Butylated Hydroxyanisole (BHA) as a substance with potential endocrine disrupting properties in cosmetic products _________________________________________________________________________________ 1 anomalies; however, skeletal examination revealed division of the thoracic vertebrae of the 2 fetuses at the highest dose. 3 Ref.: Han et al., quoted from MAK, 2012. 4 5 Diets containing 0 and 0.5% BHA (equivalent to approximately 0 and 750 mg/kg bw/day) 6 were given to mated pairs of Swiss Webster. The litters obtained from the mated pairs were 7 culled to 8 pups at birth and weaned at 21 days of age. The young were then continued on 8 a diet that was similar to that of their mothers. When the pups were 6 weeks old, 9 behavioural testing was initiated. A number of behavioural changes were observed including 10 decreased orientation reflex, decreased sleeping, decreased grooming of self, slow learning 11 and increased exploration. 12 Ref.: Stokes and Scudder, 1974, quoted from EFSA, 2011 13 14 Doses of 0, 50, 200 or 400 mg BHA/kg bw/day were given orally by gavage to groups of 15 pregnant New Zealand white rabbits from day 7 to day 18 of pregnancy. There were no 16 observed differences between the treated groups and controls in the parameters measured 17 (body weight, incidence of soft tissue or skeletal abnormalities, number of foetuses born 18 dead or alive, number of corpora lutea and implantations, general reproductive parameters). 19 The EFSA Panel concluded that a NOAEL for developmental toxicity of 400 mg/kg bw/day can 20 be derived from this study. 21 Ref.: Hansen and Meyer (1978), quoted from EFSA, 2011 22 23 A diet containing the equivalent of 0, 50, 200, or 400 mg BHA/kg bw/day was given to groups 24 of 10 young adult Danish Landrace gilt pigs The pigs were maintained on the diet for three 25 weeks and then artificially inseminated. Feeding of the diet was continued throughout the 26 study from mating (artificial insemination) to day 110 of the gestation period when the 27 foetuses were removed. No effect was seen on food consumption. A significant effect was 28 observed on the body weight of dams in the dose group given 400 mg/kg bw/day compared 29 to the control group. There was a dose-related increase in absolute and relative liver and 30 thyroid weight and absolute and relative liver and thyroid weight were statistically significantly 31 increased relative to the control at all dose levels tested. There was no effect of BHA on the 32 reproductive and developmental parameters. Anses noted that the histological picture of the 33 thyroid indicated a reduced activity which was not confirmed by other parameters. The EFSA 34 Panel concluded that a NOAEL for developmental toxicity of 400 mg/kg bw/day can be derived 35 from this study and that the NOAEL for maternal toxicity is 200 mg/kg bw/day. 36 Ref.: Hansen et al., 1982, quoted from EFSA, 2011 and Anses, 2024 37 38 The chronic ingestion of 0.5% BHA (corresponding to 750 mg/kg bw/d) by pregnant mice and 39 their offspring resulted in a variety of behavioral changes. Compared to controls, BHA-treated 40 offspring showed increased exploration, decreased sleeping, decreased self-grooming, slower 41 learning, and a decreased orientation reflex. 42 Ref.: Stokes and Scudder, 1974 43 44 Anses (2024) mentions a further, poorly reported study (Clegg, 1965) administering BHA at 45 750 mg/kg bw/d BHA on GD 1-20 (n=32 females), BHA at 750 mg/kg bw/d for 70 days before 46 pairing, continuing through pregnancy (n= 47 females) and a single administration of BHA on 47 GD 9, 11 or 13 (n=111 females) to Albino rats. BHA also administered at 500 mg/kg bw/d 48 Porton SPF rats for 7 weeks before pairing continuing during gestation; treatment commenced 49 when rats were 3 or 10 weeks old at (n=152 females). BHA was also administered to Imperial 50 Chemical Industries (ICI) SPF mice for 7 weeks before pairing, continuing until GD 18 (n=95 51 females). In mice, there were no effects on body weight, mortality rates were 2% after two 52 weeks and 25% after 7 weeks. In mice aborting after treatment with BHA there were 74 53 implantation sites, but only 40 corpora lutea of pregnancy were observed. Most of the studies were of 4 limited reliability and negative. An in vivo Comet Assay considered of limited reliability by the 5 SCCS, increased DNA migration was determined in glandular stomach and colon tissue from 6 mice (in glandular stomach at 1000 mg/kg, in colon starting at 500 mg/kg). 7 8 SCCS comment 9 Based on the observations from in vitro and in vivo studies performed with BHA, there is a 10 concern with respect to a clastogenic potential. However, the fact that positive findings were 11 observed in in vitro chromosomal aberration tests and in an in vivo comet assay has to be 12 put into perspective. Positive in vitro findings were only observed in the presence of S9, 13 indicating that metabolism might be required to exert clastogenicity. It is known from 14 literature that BHA and its metabolites (e.g. tert-butylhydroquinone) can lead to the formation 15 of reactive oxygen species in the presence of liver microsomes (Cummings and Prough, 1983; 16 Phillips et al. 1989) or that BHA could be oxidised to produce free radicals. This is underlined 17 by mechanistic investigations showing that chromosomal aberration was reduced in the 18 presence of catalase (Philipps et al., 1989). As described for other antioxidants, in living 19 organisms, the occurrence of clastogenicity will be dependent on (i) metabolism, (II) 20 exhaustion of antioxidant capacity and, last but not least, on the amounts (systemically) 21 available at the target site. 22 With respect to the positive findings observed in an in vivo comet assay performed in mice, 23 it is of note that positive findings were observed at high doses (500 and 1000 mg/kg). Such 24 doses might indeed have exhausted antioxidant capacities in the target cells, but more 25 importantly, when looking at the toxicological effects of BHA from a more holistic point of 26 view, it should be kept in mind that liver toxicity (after repeated administration) already starts 27 at much lower doses (see section 3.4.4 Repeated dose toxicity). 28 Therefore, it is most likely that a threshold mode of action can be assumed for the clastogenic 29 effects observed with BHA in vitro. Therefore, the SCCS will derive a safety calculation (MoS) 30 based on a PoD resulting from repeat dose toxicity studies (50 mg /kg bw/day). 31 32 33 33 SCCS/1682/25 Preliminary version Scientific advice on the safety of Butylated Hydroxyanisole (BHA) as a substance with potential endocrine disrupting properties in cosmetic products _________________________________________________________________________________ 1 3.4.7 Carcinogenicity 2 3 From Anses, 2024: 4 5 Several international and European assessments have been carried out on the toxicological 6 effects of BHA. No study following regulatory guideline is available. As for the other endpoints, 7 the composition of BHA was not always indicated. 8 Historic 9 - IARC reviewed BHA in October 1985 and classified it in Group 2B (Possible Human 10 Carcinogen) based on “sufficient evidence of carcinogenicity in experimental animals” and “no 11 data were available on the carcinogenicity” in human beings (IARC, 1987). In a workshop, 12 the mechanism by which BHA induces forestomach tumors in rats and was discussed and it 13 was determined that the mechanism was not relevant to humans (IARC, 2003). 14 - California Proposition 65: BHA listed on January 1, 1990 as a chemical known to the 15 State to cause cancer under the Safe Drinking Water and Toxic Enforcement Act of 1986 (this 16 decision was based on IARC). A No Significant Risk Level of 4 mg/day was established 17 (OEHHA, 1990). 18 - Netherlands environmental and public health institute, 2004: BHA is in the RIVM list of 19 514 potential CMR substances that are not on Annex 1 of 67/548/EEC (RIVM, 2004). 20 - NTP Report on Carcinogens (RoC): BHA was first listed in the Sixth Annual RoC in 1991 21 (NTP, 2016) 22 - NTP, 2016: 14th Edition: “reasonably anticipated to be a human carcinogen” based on 23 sufficient evidence of carcinogenicity from studies in experimental animals. 14th NTP RoC 24 acknowledged that the epidemiological study of stomach cancer in men and women within 25 the Netherlands showed no increase in risk at typical levels of dietary intake of BHA 26 (Botterweck et al., 2000). 27 28 Data 29 Regarding human data, the association between dietary intake of BHA and stomach cancer 30 risk was investigated in the Netherlands Cohort Study (NLCS) that started in 1986 among 31 120,852 men and women aged 55 to 69 years. A semi-quantitative food frequency 32 questionnaire was used to assess food consumption. Information on BHA content of cooking 33 fats, oils, mayonnaise and other creamy salad dressings and dried soups was obtained by 34 chemical analysis, a Dutch database of food additives (ALBA) and the Dutch Compendium of 35 Foods and Diet Products. After 6.3 years of follow-up, complete data on BHA intake of 192 36 incident stomach cancer cases and 2035 subcohort members were available for case cohort 37 analysis. Mean intake of BHA among subcohort members was 105 mg/day. For consumption 38 of mayonnaise and other creamy salad dressings with BHA, no association with stomach 39 cancer risk was observed. A statistically non-significant decrease in stomach cancer risk was 40 observed with increasing BHA intake [rate ratio (RR) highest/lowest intake of BHA = 0.57 41 (95% confidence interval (CI): 0.25- 1.30]. In this study, no significant association with 42 stomach cancer risk was found for usual intake of low levels of BHA (Botterweck et al., 2000). 43 Regarding animal data, numerous subchronic and chronic exposure studies of BHA 44 administered via food are available. The majority of these studies were conducted in rodents 45 and are prior to 2011, therefore already taken into account in pre-existing evaluations. 46 Many reviews of these studies are available in the literature: EFSA, 2011; JECFA, 1986; 1989; 47 SCF, 1989; IARC, 2003, NTP, 2016, Felter et al., 2021. 48 Overall, in rats, BHA was tested at dose levels of 0.125%-2% (55 - 1000 mg/kg bw/day). At 49 dietary concentration of 0.125% or higher, BHA led to significant incidences of forestomach 50 hyperplasia, at dietary concentration of 1% or higher significant incidences of papillomas and 51 at dietary concentration of 2% significant incidences of squamous cell carcinomas. 52 Reversibility of the hyperplastic lesions was shown to be dependent on dose and duration. In 53 a strain comparison study, the SHR rat strain was shown to be most sensitive, with the highest 54 incidence of squamous cell carcinoma. The sensitivity of the different strains was established 55 as follow: F344 rats, 26.7% (8/30); SHR rats, 76.7% (23/30); SD rats, 36.7% (11/30) and 56 Lewis rats, 6.7% (2/30) (Tamano et al., 1998). 34 SCCS/1682/25 Preliminary version Scientific advice on the safety of Butylated Hydroxyanisole (BHA) as a substance with potential endocrine disrupting properties in cosmetic products _________________________________________________________________________________ 1 Studies performed in hamsters showed proliferative changes in the forestomach including 2 induction of papillomas at a dose level of 1% BHA (1200 mg/kg bw/day). A study by Hirose 3 et al. 1990 was identified in the literature search in which it was shown that squamous cell 4 dysplasia was not reverted at a dose level of 2% BHA. 5 It was suggested that the tumorigenic action of crude BHA (the authors refer either to the 6 mixture of approximately 98% 3-BHA and 1% or 2% 2-BHA, or to the commercial mixture 7 which is a mixture of 75 to 98% 3-tert-BHA (3-BHA) and 1 to 25% 2-tert-BHA (2-BHA))on 8 the hamster forestomach was largely due to 3-BHA (Ito et al. 1986, Ito et al. 1987, Hirose et 9 al., 1986). 10 Studies performed in mice showed proliferative changes in the forestomach including 11 induction of papillomas and carcinomas at 0.5% BHA (750 mg/kg bw/day). 12 In species without a forestomach, no histopathological effects were observed. Overall, the 13 studies have included species with and without a forestomach (rats, mice, hamsters, guinea 14 pigs and dogs). Gastric epithelial hyperplasias, papillomas and carcinomas were seen in the 15 forestomach of rodents (EFSA, 2011). No tumours were observed in other tissues and organs 16 in mammals. 17 The absence of a homologue tissue for the forestomach in humans makes it difficult to 18 extrapolate these observations to humans. The question of the relevance of this tumour type 19 for human hazard has been extensively discussed in the early 2000’s. It was noted that if 20 humans do not have a forestomach, they possess histologically similar organs, including the 21 oral cavity, pharynx, oesophagus, and glandular stomach. The potential risk from non- 22 genotoxic forestomach carcinogens for humans involves exposure of the mouth, pharynx, and 23 oesophagus at dose levels that exert irritating action. 24 It is assumed that exposure to non-genotoxic chemicals at concentrations far below those 25 having irritating potential is not hazardous to humans (Wester et al., 1988). IARC (2003) 26 discussed that non-DNA reactive agents appear to cause forestomach tumours primarily 27 through initial cytotoxicity and subsequent sustained cell proliferation and hyperplasia. 28 IARC (2003) also recognises that the relevance for humans is probably limited for agents that 29 have no demonstrable genotoxicity and that are solely carcinogenic for the forestomach 30 squamous epithelium in rodents after oral administration. This is because the experimental 31 exposure conditions during oral administration in animals (particularly with gavage dosing) 32 are quite different compared to human exposure. In experimental animals, high local 33 exposure concentrations of test substance in the forestomach and prolonged exposure of the 34 epithelial tissue may have physical effects. Consequently, for these agents, the carcinogenic 35 mode of action might be specific to experimental animals. IARC therefore recommends that, 36 in evaluating the relevance of the induction of forestomach tumours in rodents for human 37 cancer, the exposure conditions in the experiments have to be considered (IARC 2003, shared 38 by RIVM, 2004). In this review, IARC also looked at some substances in particular. Indeed, 39 they concluded that BHA induced only squamous-cell tumours of the forestomach in three 40 rodent species. At high concentrations, the mode of action by which BHA produces 41 forestomach tumours may involve a net production of free radicals during the long transit 42 time in the forestomach, resulting in cytotoxicity and subsequent hyperplasia. Upon chronic 43 administration of BHA, this hyperplasia is sustained, which leads to a tumour-promoting effect 44 specific to the forestomach. 45 In more recent literature, it was shown that such chemicals should be evaluated in detail 46 before discarding continuous induction of cell proliferation, hyperplasia, and ultimately 47 carcinomas. The genotoxicity studies indicate a lack of potential for BHA to induce mutations 48 or interaction with or damage DNA directly, the effects observed being secondary to oxidative 49 stress. 50 Overall, BHA induces proliferative changes in the forestomach of rodents.
